rv.q: It's a remarkable picture of restlessness and need, and reason enough to see Cullman's staging.
Unfortunately, even Tomei’s vivifying, staunchly committed performance isn’t enough to keep this ripe comedy at the emotional heights it needs to sustain.
A burlesque of desire, directed by Trip Cullman with desperate energy and garbled sense of time and place, it has the buoyancy of a leaky balloon that makes rude noises as it deflates.
Although the tone of the play and production waver too much to leave a permament impression, The Rose Tattoo has an interesting position in the Williams canon.
Strange, if not exactly lovely.
Allowing for Serafina’s tendency to hyperbole, she might be talking about the production in which she appears.
Instead, it’s shrill and hysterically over the top, poorly paced and blighted by some very large Italianate acting with all the authenticity of an Olive Garden chicken alfredo.
Its focus can feel woolly and puzzling (and we leave Hwang and his stabbing in a way-too-long dramatic limbo), but its mischief and intelligence powerfully root it.
Despite winning the Tony for Best Play in 1951, The Rose Tattoo still feels like one of Williams’ lesser works, missing the thunder and heat of his legendary ones.
If happily ever after is better than a shattered glass unicorn or getting carted off to the neighborhood loony bin, it probably shouldn’t feel less fun.
It is wonderful enough where it really counts to overcome its mostly insignificant shortcomings.
It's a testament to the two stars that despite the production's shortcomings, they make it all worthwhile.
Another way of putting this is to maintain that Williams’ insistence on the play’s profundities is set aside for a production that skims the text’s surface and is content to do only that.
What it does not deserve is the pink-flamingos revival that opened Tuesday at Broadway’s Theatre, a presentation of the Roundabout Theatre Company.
The Roundabout production of The Rose Tattoo is most useful in letting us understand why there have been so relatively few Broadway revivals of this play.

Though Williams specifies the presence of a guitar-playing Sicilian folk singer between scenes, Cullman here expands that stage direction into a distracting wandering female Greek chorus. There’s also the much smaller matter of the live goat, which was probably done away with for practical reasons.
In more comic mode, Marisa Tomei gives us a passionate, sensual, and sexy Serafina Delle Rose.
Tomei adeptly navigates through passages of gravitas to find humor, and her chemistry with Elliott’s Alvaro is seductive and charming.
Unfortunately, neither direction nor casting can do much for the rest of The Rose Tattoo, which includes a bunch of supporting roles that are underbaked, overdrawn, or just plain forgettable.
Stretched too broadly and the whole business can warp.
This Tennessee Williams is sugar coated.
She is a light-opera soubrette cast in a role meant for a Wagnerian soprano.
What she can’t do single-handedly, though, is save us completely from Cullman’s deeply questionable directorial choices.
